title: Portfolio and GitHub that get noticed
intro: A strong portfolio is not about having the most projects; it is about making your best work easy to understand and verify. In this lesson, you will learn how recruiters and tech leads evaluate a developer's online presence quickly, and how to turn your capstone into evidence of real engineering ability.
body:
## What gets noticed in 30 seconds

Imagine that a recruiter receives your application and opens your GitHub profile or portfolio. They may not spend ten minutes exploring it immediately. The first few seconds are usually spent answering very simple questions:

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "The 30-second scan", "steps": [{"label": "Profile", "sub": "photo, headline, pinned repos"}, {"label": "README", "sub": "what it does, screenshot"}, {"label": "Live demo", "sub": "does it work?"}, {"label": "Code", "sub": "structure, tests, commits"}]}
~~~

- What kind of developer is this?
- Does this person actually build things?
- Is the work relevant to the role?
- Can I quickly understand one or two projects?
- Does the developer appear careful and professional?

A tech lead is likely to look at the same information from a different perspective. They may care about architecture, code quality, testing, decisions, documentation, and whether the project looks like something the developer could maintain in a real team.

This means your portfolio should not make the visitor hunt for evidence. **Your best work should be visible, understandable, and easy to verify.**

A good portfolio does not need dozens of projects. Two or three strong projects with excellent documentation can be much more convincing than twenty unfinished repositories.

## Your GitHub profile is part of your portfolio

Your GitHub profile is often the first technical evidence someone sees. Treat it as a professional landing page rather than an automatically generated list of repositories.

Start with a clear profile description. Someone should understand your main technologies and the type of work you are interested in without reading your entire profile.

For example:

~~~text
Full-stack developer focused on Java, Spring Boot, React, TypeScript and PostgreSQL.
I build practical web applications with an emphasis on clean APIs, testing and deployment.
~~~

Avoid turning the description into a list of every technology you have ever touched. A focused profile communicates more confidence.

## Pin your strongest repositories

GitHub lets you pin repositories to your profile. Use this space strategically.

Your pinned repositories should answer a simple question: **What work do you want a technical person to see first?**

For a junior or career-changing developer, a strong selection could include:

1. Your full-stack capstone.
2. Another project demonstrating a different important skill.
3. A smaller project demonstrating a technical specialty.
4. An open-source contribution or particularly interesting experiment.

You do not have to pin repositories simply because they are your newest projects. Pin the projects that best represent the developer you want to be hired as.

A repository that demonstrates a complete React + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL application can be more valuable than a repository containing fifty isolated coding exercises.

## Write a profile README

A profile README gives you space to introduce yourself before someone starts browsing repositories.

Keep it readable. A useful structure is:

~~~text
# Your Name

Short professional introduction.

## What I work with
- Java / Spring Boot
- React / TypeScript
- PostgreSQL
- Docker

## Featured projects
Links to your strongest repositories.

## Currently learning
One or two relevant areas.

## Contact
Portfolio and LinkedIn links.
~~~

Do not turn the README into a wall of badges. A few useful links are better than dozens of decorative icons.

The profile README should complement your portfolio, not duplicate every paragraph from it.

## The project README matters even more

A repository with good code but no documentation creates unnecessary friction. A reviewer should be able to understand the project without reverse-engineering your source code.

A strong project README should normally explain:

- What problem the project solves.
- Who the intended user is.
- What the application does.
- What the main technologies are.
- How to see the application running.
- How to run it locally.
- How to run the tests.
- Important architectural or technical decisions.
- Known limitations.

The README is not a school assignment. It is the front door to your code.

## Start with the problem

Do not begin with a huge technology list.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Forgettable", "lang": "markdown", "code": "# portal\nSpring Boot + React project.\nRun with mvn.", "note": "No problem, no proof, no way to try it."}, "right": {"title": "Memorable", "lang": "markdown", "code": "# Customer portal\nCustomers track orders and get support\nwithout email ping-pong.\n\n▶ Live demo · 📸 screenshot\nStack: React · Spring Boot · PostgreSQL\nRun: docker compose up", "note": "Problem first, then proof, then a one-line start."}}
~~~

Compare these two introductions:

~~~text
Bad:

This project uses React, TypeScript, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, JWT, Docker,
Flyway, JUnit, Testcontainers and GitHub Actions.
~~~

~~~text
Better:

The customer portal gives customers one place to view their orders and invoices,
open support tickets, and communicate with the support team. Administrators can
manage incoming tickets from a protected admin interface.
~~~

The second version explains why the software exists. The technology stack can follow afterward.

Hiring teams want evidence that you understand software as a solution to a problem, not just as a collection of frameworks.

## Add a screenshot or GIF

A screenshot lets someone understand the result immediately. A short GIF can demonstrate an interaction such as creating a ticket, filtering a list, or completing a workflow.

For a full-stack application, consider showing:

- The main dashboard.
- A meaningful business workflow.
- A form and its validation.
- An administrative screen.

Do not fill the README with twenty screenshots. Pick the images that explain the application best.

If the project is interactive, a short demonstration can be especially useful because it proves that the interface is not merely a static mockup.

## Provide a live demo

A deployment link is powerful evidence because it lets someone verify the project immediately.

Your README can contain a prominent link such as:

~~~text
Live demo: https://example.com
~~~

Make sure the link actually works.

If the demo requires authentication, explain how to access it. For example, provide a deliberately created demo account with limited permissions rather than exposing a real personal account.

If the project cannot reasonably be deployed publicly, explain why and provide clear local setup instructions instead.

A broken demo link is worse than no demo link because it suggests the project is not being maintained.

## Explain the technology stack

The technology section should help the reader understand the architecture.

For the customer portal, you might write:

~~~text
Frontend
- React
- TypeScript
- Vite

Backend
- Java 21
- Spring Boot
- Spring Security

Data
- PostgreSQL
- Flyway

Infrastructure
- Docker Compose
- GitHub Actions
~~~

You can add one sentence explaining why an important technology was selected. Avoid writing a paragraph for every dependency.

## Make local setup genuinely reproducible

A good README should let another developer start the project without guessing.

For a Docker Compose project, a setup section might look like:

~~~text
## Running locally

Requirements:
- Docker
- Docker Compose

Start the stack:

docker compose up --build

The frontend is available at:
http://localhost:5173

The backend is available at:
http://localhost:8080
~~~

Then explain required environment variables and test commands.

Do not assume that because you remember how the project works, another person will know it too. Documentation is successful when someone unfamiliar with the project can follow it.

## Document testing

Testing is valuable evidence for a developer portfolio because it demonstrates that you think beyond the happy path.

Your README could explain:

~~~text
## Tests

Backend unit and integration tests:
./mvnw test

Frontend tests:
npm test

End-to-end tests:
npm run test:e2e
~~~

You do not need an enormous test suite simply for portfolio purposes. What matters is that the tests cover meaningful behavior and that the commands actually work.

If you use Testcontainers, explain briefly that integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL container rather than only mocked database behavior.

## Explain important decisions

A project becomes much more interesting when you explain decisions rather than merely listing technologies.

For example:

~~~text
## Technical decisions

JWT is used for API authentication because the frontend and backend are deployed
as separate applications and the API needs a stateless authentication mechanism.

Flyway manages schema changes so local and production databases can be upgraded
through version-controlled migrations.

Ticket messages initially use normal HTTP requests rather than WebSockets because
real-time communication is not required for the MVP.
~~~

This demonstrates engineering judgment.

You do not need to claim that your choice is universally best. Explain the context, the trade-off, and why the decision was reasonable for your project.

## Commit history tells a story

A repository's commit history can reveal how you work.

Compare:

~~~text
final
final2
fix
changes
really-final
~~~

with:

~~~text
feat(auth): add JWT login endpoint
feat(orders): add customer order API
feat(tickets): create ticket workflow
feat(frontend): add protected customer routes
fix(tickets): enforce customer ownership
 test(api): cover ticket authorization
~~~

The second history communicates a development process.

You do not need perfect conventional commits for every project, but commits should have understandable purposes. Avoid combining unrelated changes into enormous commits whenever possible.

## Pull requests are evidence too

If you work alone, you can still use pull requests for larger features. Create a branch, implement the feature, open a pull request, review your own changes, and merge it.

A useful pull request description might contain:

~~~text
## What changed
Added customer ticket creation and listing.

## Why
Customers need to open and track support requests.

## Testing
- Unit tests
- Controller tests
- Manual browser test

## Notes
Customer ownership is checked in the service layer.
~~~

This creates evidence that you understand review-oriented development rather than simply pushing directly to the default branch.

## Issues should represent useful work

A GitHub issue can represent a feature, bug, technical improvement, or decision that needs attention.

Good issue:

~~~text
Add authorization check for ticket messages

Customers must only be able to read and create messages belonging
to tickets they own. Admins can access all tickets.

Acceptance criteria:
- Customer can access own ticket messages.
- Customer receives 403 for another customer's ticket.
- Admin can access any ticket.
~~~

Weak issue:

~~~text
Fix security stuff
~~~

Specific issues make your project history easier to understand and can demonstrate that you know how to break requirements into actionable work.

## A one-page portfolio site

Your portfolio site should make the best information accessible quickly. It does not need ten pages.

A strong one-page structure could be:

~~~text
Hero
  ↓
About / positioning
  ↓
Featured projects
  ↓
Skills
  ↓
Selected case studies
  ↓
Contact
~~~

The hero should communicate who you are and what you build.

The projects section should contain your strongest evidence rather than every experiment you have ever made.

Keep navigation simple. Someone should be able to understand your profile without clicking through five levels of menus.

## Write case studies, not just project descriptions

A case study explains the journey from problem to solution.

A useful structure is:

### Problem

What problem existed? Who experienced it? Why did it matter?

### Constraints

What limitations affected the solution? Time, budget, existing systems, technical requirements, or scope?

### Solution

What did you build? Explain the important parts without drowning the reader in implementation details.

### Technical decisions

Why did you choose your architecture, database, authentication approach, or deployment model?

### Challenges

What went wrong or required the most reasoning?

### Result

What can users do now? What improved? What did you learn?

For example, instead of saying “I built a ticket system with Spring Boot,” you could explain that customers previously had no central place to track support conversations, so you created a protected ticket workflow with ownership checks, persistent messages, automated tests, and a deployed React interface.

That tells a much stronger story.

## Connect the capstone to your professional profile

Your GitHub, portfolio, and LinkedIn profile should tell compatible stories.

If LinkedIn says you are a full-stack Java and React developer but your GitHub profile is dominated by unrelated beginner tutorials, there is a disconnect.

Your strongest project should appear consistently across the profiles:

~~~text
Portfolio
→ Customer Portal case study

GitHub
→ Customer Portal repository

LinkedIn
→ Customer Portal project / featured link
~~~

The wording does not need to be identical. The important thing is that the same evidence supports the same professional positioning.

Your LinkedIn profile should also link to your portfolio and GitHub where appropriate. Your portfolio should link back to the profiles where people can verify your work.

## Common mistakes

### Tutorial clones

Following a tutorial is useful for learning, but a repository that is obviously copied from a tutorial is weak portfolio evidence.

If you build a tutorial project, customize it substantially. Add your own requirements, solve a different problem, change the architecture where appropriate, add tests, deploy it, and explain your decisions.

The goal is to demonstrate what you can build without a tutorial holding your hand.

### No README

A repository with no README forces visitors to inspect the code just to understand what the project is. That creates unnecessary friction.

### Broken links

Check every deployment, GitHub, LinkedIn, screenshot, and documentation link. A portfolio should be tested like a product.

### Too many projects

Ten mediocre projects do not necessarily communicate more skill than two excellent ones. Curate aggressively.

### Technology soup

Listing twenty technologies does not prove expertise. Explain what you actually used and why.

### Overdesigned portfolio

Animations can make a portfolio memorable, but they should not make it difficult to navigate. A hiring manager is not evaluating your ability to build a loading screen.

### No evidence of engineering practices

A polished screenshot alone does not demonstrate full-stack ability. Show tests, API design, Docker, CI, deployment, architecture decisions, and security where they are genuinely part of the project.

## Turn the capstone into evidence

Your customer portal is particularly useful because it can demonstrate an entire development lifecycle.

You can show:

- User stories and acceptance criteria.
- A relational data model.
- REST API design.
- Spring Security and JWT authentication.
- React routing and state management.
- DTOs and validation.
- PostgreSQL and Flyway migrations.
- Unit and integration tests.
- Docker Compose.
- CI with GitHub Actions.
- Deployment and environment configuration.
- Logging and monitoring.
- A production-style README.

This is much stronger than saying “I know Spring Boot and React.” Your project becomes evidence supporting that statement.

## A final portfolio checklist

Before putting the capstone on your portfolio, open the site as if you were a recruiter seeing it for the first time.

Can you identify the developer in five seconds?

Can you find the strongest project immediately?

Can you understand what problem the project solves?

Can you see a screenshot or live demo?

Can you open the source repository?

Can you understand how to run it?

Can you find tests and technical decisions?

Do the deployment and GitHub links work?

Does the GitHub repository look maintained and understandable?

Can you find the same project on LinkedIn?

If the answer is yes, your portfolio is doing its job. It is not trying to convince someone with marketing language. It is **making good technical evidence easy to find**.

That is the real purpose of a developer portfolio: reduce the distance between saying “I can build this” and allowing someone to verify that you actually did.
takeaways: Make your strongest technical evidence visible within seconds.
Use pinned repositories and profile README content strategically.
A project README should explain the problem, result, setup, tests, and important decisions.
Commit history, issues, and pull requests can demonstrate how you work.
Use case studies to explain problems, constraints, decisions, challenges, and results.
Keep your portfolio, GitHub, and LinkedIn aligned around the same professional story.

quiz.question: What should a recruiter ideally understand within the first few seconds of seeing your portfolio?
options: Every technology you have ever used.
Your complete employment history.
Who you are, what you build, and where your strongest evidence is.
The internal architecture of your largest project.
quiz.explanation: The first few seconds should establish your professional positioning and make your strongest work easy to find.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a strong project README?
options: To make visitors reverse-engineer the source code.
To explain the problem, result, technology, setup, testing, and important decisions.
To list as many dependencies and badges as possible.
To replace the project's automated tests.
quiz.explanation: A README is the front door to the repository. It should give another developer enough context to understand and run the project.

quiz.question: Which project description provides the strongest evidence of engineering ability?
options: A list of twenty frameworks used in the project.
A screenshot with no explanation.
A statement that the project was built during a coding course.
A case study explaining the problem, constraints, technical decisions, challenges, and result.
quiz.explanation: A case study demonstrates reasoning and engineering judgment rather than merely listing technologies.

quiz.question: Why can commit history be useful to a tech lead reviewing a portfolio project?
options: It can provide evidence of how the developer organizes and evolves work.
It proves that every line of code was written without an IDE.
It automatically proves that the application is secure.
It guarantees that the project has no bugs.
quiz.explanation: A clear commit history can show coherent development increments, meaningful changes, and an understandable engineering process.

quiz.question: Which is a common portfolio mistake?
options: Linking a working live demo.
Explaining how to run the project with Docker Compose.
Showing a tutorial clone without adding meaningful original work.
Documenting important technical decisions.
quiz.explanation: Tutorials are useful for learning, but an unchanged tutorial clone provides weak evidence of independent problem solving.

exercise.title: Build a portfolio project section
exercise.task:
Write a complete HTML page. Define exactly the page itself; there are no required JavaScript function names for this exercise. The page must have exactly one `h1` containing the person's name. Add a `section` with `id="projects"` containing at least two `article` elements with class `project`. Each project article must contain an `h3`, a `p` with class `summary` containing at least 40 characters, an `img` with a non-empty `alt` attribute, a `ul` with class `tech` containing at least three `li` elements, a link whose visible text is `Live demo`, and a link whose visible text is `Source code` with an `href` starting with `https://github.com/`. Every link with `target="_blank"` must have a `rel` attribute containing `noopener`. The root `html` element must have a non-empty `lang` attribute, and the page must contain a `meta` element with `name="description"` and non-empty `content`.

Write the page as real portfolio content rather than placeholders. You may use your own project names, descriptions, screenshots, and GitHub paths, as long as the required structure and attributes are present.

exercise.hint: Build the document structure first: `html` with `lang`, `head` with the description metadata, exactly one `h1`, and a `section` with the required ID. Then make each project article follow the same checklist. When you use `target="_blank"`, include `noopener` in `rel` to avoid the security problem associated with opening a new browsing context.
